core_message: The dashboard is not mainly about memorizing microbe names. It is about understanding what soil life may be doing: recycling nutrients, building structure, helping roots, storing carbon, and responding to drought or wetness.

soil_food_web_steps.title: Plants feed the soil
soil_food_web_steps.simple: Plants leak sugars and other compounds from their roots. This feeds bacteria and fungi near the roots.
soil_food_web_steps.dashboard_connection: When the dashboard talks about root zones, nutrient cycling, or microbial function, this is the living plant-soil exchange behind it.

soil_food_web_steps.title: Microbes recycle dead material
soil_food_web_steps.simple: Bacteria and fungi break down leaves, roots, mulch, and compost into smaller pieces and nutrients.
soil_food_web_steps.dashboard_connection: Carbon decomposition and product-name signals help show this kind of breakdown potential.

soil_food_web_steps.title: Predators release nutrients
soil_food_web_steps.simple: Tiny soil animals such as protozoa and nematodes eat microbes. When they do, nutrients are released in plant-available forms.
soil_food_web_steps.dashboard_connection: The current dashboard does not directly measure these predators, but nutrient-cycling signals help explain why a full soil food web matters.

soil_food_web_steps.title: Fungi and roots build structure
soil_food_web_steps.simple: Fungal threads, roots, organic matter, and clay help soil form aggregates. Aggregates improve water movement, air, and habitat.
soil_food_web_steps.dashboard_connection: Clay, organic matter, biofilm/motility signals, and soil texture are clues about structure and habitat.

soil_food_web_steps.title: Soil conditions choose the community
soil_food_web_steps.simple: Shallow limestone, heavy clay, deep loam, wet lowlands, and dry uplands all favor different living communities.
soil_food_web_steps.dashboard_connection: The soil map is the local habitat layer. Regional microbial data help explain what kinds of biological jobs may fit similar soils.

transport_secretion.plain_meaning: Microbes need to move food, minerals, and chemical messages in and out of their cells.
transport_secretion.why_gardeners_care: Active exchange around roots is part of a living soil system.
transport_secretion.how_to_use: Treat this as a broad sign of microbial activity potential, not a direct gardening instruction.

phosphorus_cycle.friendly_title: Making phosphorus easier for plants to use
phosphorus_cycle.plain_meaning: Phosphorus is important for roots, flowers, seeds, and plant energy. Some microbes help shift phosphorus between locked-up and available forms.
phosphorus_cycle.why_gardeners_care: In alkaline limestone soils, phosphorus can be present but hard for plants to access.
phosphorus_cycle.how_to_use: Support roots and organic matter; avoid assuming more fertilizer is always the answer.

metal_iron.plain_meaning: Microbes interact with iron and other minerals in soil.
metal_iron.why_gardeners_care: Mineral interactions can affect nutrient availability and soil chemistry.
metal_iron.how_to_use: Think of this as mineral-soil chemistry context, not a stand-alone plant recommendation.

stress_drought_heat.plain_meaning: Some microbes carry genes that help them survive hard conditions like drying, heat, or oxidative stress.
stress_drought_heat.why_gardeners_care: Central Texas soils often swing between wet and dry. Stress-tolerant soil life may matter in restoration.
stress_drought_heat.how_to_use: Protect soil cover, roots, mulch/leaf litter, and organic matter to buffer extremes.

motility_biofilm.friendly_title: Living around roots and soil particles
motility_biofilm.plain_meaning: Some microbes move through water films or form biofilms on roots and soil particles.
motility_biofilm.why_gardeners_care: Biofilms and root-zone life can help create stable microhabitats.
motility_biofilm.how_to_use: Avoid unnecessary disturbance and keep living roots in the soil when possible.

sulfur_cycle.plain_meaning: Sulfur is a plant nutrient and part of soil chemistry.
sulfur_cycle.why_gardeners_care: Sulfur cycling is one piece of the larger nutrient web.
sulfur_cycle.how_to_use: Use as a background soil-function clue, not a reason to add sulfur without a soil test.

nitrogen_cycle.plain_meaning: Nitrogen supports leafy growth. Microbes help transform nitrogen into different forms.
nitrogen_cycle.why_gardeners_care: Too much fertilizer can disrupt plant communities, especially native plantings.
nitrogen_cycle.how_to_use: Favor plant diversity, roots, organic matter, and soil cover before reaching for fertilizer.

carbon_decomposition.plain_meaning: Microbes help turn dead roots, leaves, mulch, and compost into soil organic matter and nutrients.
carbon_decomposition.why_gardeners_care: This is the engine of the soil food web.
carbon_decomposition.how_to_use: Keep leaf litter where appropriate, use mulch wisely, and reduce disturbance.

carbon_fixation.plain_meaning: Some microbes may have genes related to capturing carbon.
carbon_fixation.why_gardeners_care: Carbon is part of soil structure and long-term soil health.
carbon_fixation.how_to_use: Do not overinterpret this alone. Pair it with plant cover, roots, organic matter, and soil protection.

simple_actions.action: Keep living roots in the soil
simple_actions.why: Roots feed microbes and help build soil structure.
simple_actions.example: Use native perennials, grasses, and mixed plantings rather than bare soil.

simple_actions.why: Soil cover protects microbes from heat, erosion, and drying.
simple_actions.example: Use leaf litter, mulch, cover plants, or dense native planting where appropriate.

simple_actions.why: Repeated digging and compaction can break soil structure and fungal networks.
simple_actions.example: Avoid working clay soil when wet and reduce unnecessary tilling.

simple_actions.why: Organic matter feeds decomposers, but too much compost or fertilizer can shift plant communities.
simple_actions.example: Use soil tests for fertility decisions and avoid over-amending native plant sites.

simple_actions.why: Plants adapted to shallow limestone, clay, upland, or riparian soils will usually perform better.
simple_actions.example: Use the map and soil clues before choosing a planting palette.

what_the_dashboard_can_say: This soil setting may support certain soil-life functions.
Regional data show functional potential related to nutrient cycling, stress tolerance, decomposition, and soil structure.
The soil map suggests likely habitat conditions.
This is useful for planning and education.
what_the_dashboard_should_not_say: This exact yard has these microbes.
This proves the function is active right now.
This tells you exactly how much fertilizer to apply.
